claim: The fitness landscape of four sites in protein GB1 contains 204 = 160,000 variants.
source: In this study, we investigated the fitness landscape of all variants (204 = 160,000) at four amino acid sites (V39, D40, G41 and V54) in an epistatic region of protein G domain B1 (GB1, 56 amino acids in total) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), an immunoglobulin-binding protein expressed in Streptococcal bacteria (Sjöbring et al., 1991; Sauer-Eriksson et al., 1995).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of variants and provides the calculation (204 = 160,000).

claim: The four chosen sites (V39, D40, G41, V54) contain 12 of the top 20 positively epistatic interactions among all pairwise interactions in protein GB1.
source: The four chosen sites contain 12 of the top 20 positively epistatic interactions among all pairwise interactions in protein GB1, as we previously characterized (Olson et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by reference to previous work (Olson et al., 2014) and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 2.4% of mutants in the fitness landscape were beneficial (fitness > 1).
source: While most mutants had a lower fitness compared to WT (fitness < 1), 2.4% of mutants were beneficial (fitness > 1). (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Sign epistasis and reciprocal sign epistasis are prevalent in the fitness landscape.
source: Indeed, we found that these two types of epistasis were prevalent in our fitness landscape (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing the fraction of different types of epistasis.

claim: The number of selectively inaccessible direct paths is positively correlated with the ruggedness induced by pairwise epistasis.
source: As expected, the number of selectively inaccessible direct paths, i.e. paths that involve fitness declines, was found to be positively correlated with the ruggedness induced by pairwise epistasis (Figure 1—figure supplement 6, Pearson correlation = 0.66, p=1.0 × 10−4) (Poelwijk et al., 2007).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with statistical support (Pearson correlation and p-value) and referenced to Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: More than 40% of reciprocal sign epistasis can be circumvented by at least one conversion bypass.
source: More than 40% of the time there was at least one successful conversion bypass and in many cases multiple bypasses were available (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2B showing the distribution of conversion bypasses.

claim: Detour bypass has a lower probability of success than conversion bypass.
source: Detour bypass was observed in our system (Figure 2D), but was not as prevalent and had a lower probability of success than conversion bypass.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by Figure 2D.

claim: Out of 38 possible detour bypasses for a chosen reciprocal sign epistasis, there were on average 1.2 conversion bypasses and 0.27 detour bypasses available.
source: Out of 38 possible detour bypasses for a chosen reciprocal sign epistasis, we found that there were on average 1.2 conversion bypasses and 0.27 detour bypasses available.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with specific numerical values.

claim: Higher-order epistasis is necessary for two of the three possible scenarios where detour bypass can occur.
source: We proved that higher-order epistasis is necessary for the scenario that reciprocal sign epistasis is changed to magnitude epistasis, as well as for one of the two scenarios that reciprocal sign epistasis is changed to sign epistasis (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and proven in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Higher-order interactions are enriched among specific amino acid combinations of sites 39, 41 and 54.
source: The skewed composition of amino acids in these subgraphs indicates that higher-order interactions are enriched among specific amino acid combinations of site 39, 41 and 54.
evidence: This is stated based on the sequence logo analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The interaction among sites 39, 41, and 54 is consistent with the protein structure, where the side chains of these sites can physically interact with each other at the core.
source: This interaction among 3 sites is consistent with our knowledge of the protein structure, where the side chains of sites 39, 41, and 54 can physically interact with each other at the core (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) and destabilize the protein due to steric effects (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated based on structural knowledge and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: G41L and V54H were positively epistatic when site 39 was isoleucine [I], but the interaction changed to negative epistasis when site 39 carried a tyrosine [Y] or a tryptophan [W].
source: For example, G41L and V54H were positively epistatic when site 39 was isoleucine [I], but the interaction changed to negative epistasis when site 39 carried a tyrosine [Y] or a tryptophan [W] (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 3C-D showing the epistasis values.

claim: In the complete sequence space, there are a total of 30 fitness peaks (local maxima).
source: In the complete sequence space, we identified a total of 30 fitness peaks (i.e. local maxima); among them 15 peaks had fitness larger than WT and their combined basins of attraction covered 99% of the sequence space (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: 15 fitness peaks had fitness larger than WT and their combined basins of attraction covered 99% of the sequence space.
source: In the complete sequence space, we identified a total of 30 fitness peaks (i.e. local maxima); among them 15 peaks had fitness larger than WT and their combined basins of attraction covered 99% of the sequence space (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 4A.

claim: Conversion was found to be pervasive during adaptation in the fitness landscape (17% of mutational steps for Greedy Model, 41% for Correlated Fixation Model, 59% for Equal Fixation Model).
source: Conversion was found to be pervasive during adaptation in our fitness landscape (17% of mutational steps for Greedy Model, 41% for Correlated Fixation Model, 59% for Equal Fixation Model).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with specific percentages for each model.

claim: Indirect paths increased the number of genotypes with access to each fitness peak.
source: Indeed, we found that indirect paths increased the number of genotypes with access to each fitness peak (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 4E.

claim: The fraction of genotypes with accessible paths to all 15 fitness peaks increased from 34% to 93% when indirect adaptive paths were allowed.
source: In addition, the fraction of genotypes with accessible paths to all 15 fitness peaks increased from from 34% to 93% when indirect adaptive paths were allowed (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with specific percentages and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claim: A substantial fraction of beneficial variants (fitness > 1) in the sequence space were accessible from WT only if indirect paths were used.
source: We also found that a substantial fraction of beneficial variants (fitness > 1) in the sequence space were accessible from WT only if indirect paths were used (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 4F.

claim: The fitness measurements in this study were highly consistent with a previous study on the fitness of single and double mutants in protein GB1 (Pearson correlation = 0.97).
source: The fitness measurements in this study were highly consistent with our previous study on the fitness of single and double mutants in protein GB1 (Pearson correlation = 0.97, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B) (Olson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with a Pearson correlation value and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: 93.4% of all variants had fitness values computed from the sequencing data.
source: We were able to compute the fitness for 93.4% of all variants from the sequencing data.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The fitness values for 10,639 variants (6.6% of the entire sequence space) were not directly measured or were filtered out because of low read counts.
source: The fitness values for 10,639 variants (6.6% of the entire sequence space) were not directly measured (read count in the input pool = 0) or were filtered out because of low read counts in the input pool (see section "Calculation of fitness").
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The model-predicted fitness values were highly correlated with the actual fitness values (Pearson correlation=0.93).
source: For measured variants, the model-predicted fitness values were highly correlated with the actual fitness values (Pearson correlation=0.93, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with a Pearson correlation value and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Protein GB1 is an immunoglobulin-binding protein expressed in Streptococcal bacteria.
source: In this study, we investigated the fitness landscape of all variants (204 = 160,000) at four amino acid sites (V39, D40, G41 and V54) in an epistatic region of protein G domain B1 (GB1, 56 amino acids in total) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), an immunoglobulin-binding protein expressed in Streptococcal bacteria (Sjöbring et al., 1991; Sauer-Eriksson et al., 1995).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Sjöbring et al., 1991; Sauer-Eriksson et al., 1995).

claim: The fitness of protein GB1 variants is determined by both stability (the fraction of folded proteins) and function (binding affinity to IgG-Fc).
source: The "fitness" of protein GB1 variants, as determined by both stability (i.e. the fraction of folded proteins) and function (i.e. binding affinity to IgG-Fc), was measured in a high-throughput manner by coupling mRNA display with Illumina sequencing (see Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 3) (Roberts and Szostak, 1997; Olson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by citations (Roberts and Szostak, 1997; Olson et al., 2012).

claim: The number of selectively accessible paths varied from 12 to 1 among the 29 subgraphs analyzed.
source: Out of 24 possible direct paths, the number of selectively accessible paths (i.e. with monotonically increasing fitness) varied from 12 to 1 among the 29 subgraphs (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 1B.

claim: In the most extreme case, only one path was accessible from WT to the quadruple mutant WLFA.
source: In the most extreme case, only one path was accessible from WT to the quadruple mutant WLFA (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 1A.

claim: There was a substantial skew in the computed probability of realization among accessible direct paths.
source: We also observed a substantial skew in the computed probability of realization among accessible direct paths (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), suggesting that most of the realizations in adaptation were captured by a small fraction of possible trajectories (Weinreich et al., 2006).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 5 and a citation (Weinreich et al., 2006).

claim: Most of the realizations in adaptation were captured by a small fraction of possible trajectories.
source: We also observed a substantial skew in the computed probability of realization among accessible direct paths (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), suggesting that most of the realizations in adaptation were captured by a small fraction of possible trajectories (Weinreich et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the observed skew in probability of realization and supported by a citation (Weinreich et al., 2006).

claim: The maximum number of possible conversion bypasses is always fixed at 19×2-2=36.
source: While the maximum number of possible conversion bypasses is always fixed (19×2-2=36), the maximum number of possible detour bypasses (19 × (L − 2)) is proportional to the sequence length L of the entire protein (whereas our study uses a subset L = 4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with the calculation provided.

claim: The maximum number of possible detour bypasses (19 × (L − 2)) is proportional to the sequence length L of the entire protein.
source: While the maximum number of possible conversion bypasses is always fixed (19×2-2=36), the maximum number of possible detour bypasses (19 × (L − 2)) is proportional to the sequence length L of the entire protein (whereas our study uses a subset L = 4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated with the formula provided.

claim: The pervasiveness of extra-dimensional bypasses contrasts with the prevailing view that adaptive evolution is often blocked by reciprocal sign epistasis when only direct paths of adaptation are considered.
source: The pervasiveness of extra-dimensional bypasses in our system contrasts with the prevailing view that adaptive evolution is often blocked by reciprocal sign epistasis, when only direct paths of adaptation are considered.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a contrast to the prevailing view.

claim: Higher-order epistasis has been reported in a few biological systems.
source: Higher-order epistasis has been reported in a few biological systems (Wang et al., 2013; Pettersson et al., 2011; Palmer et al., 2015), and is likely to be common in nature (Weinreich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Wang et al., 2013; Pettersson et al., 2011; Palmer et al., 2015; Weinreich et al., 2013).

claim: Higher-order epistasis is likely to be common in nature.
source: Higher-order epistasis has been reported in a few biological systems (Wang et al., 2013; Pettersson et al., 2011; Palmer et al., 2015), and is likely to be common in nature (Weinreich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a likelihood and supported by a citation (Weinreich et al., 2013).

claim: Higher-order epistasis can either increase or decrease the ruggedness induced by pairwise epistasis.
source: Our results suggest that higher-order epistasis can either increase or decrease the ruggedness induced by pairwise epistasis, which in turn determines the accessibility of direct paths in a rugged fitness landscape (Figure 3—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the results and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 6.

claim: Higher-order epistasis plays an important role in mediating detour bypass.
source: We also revealed the important role of higher-order epistasis in mediating detour bypass, which could promote evolutionary accessibility via indirect paths.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a finding of the work.

claim: Even in the most rugged regions of a protein fitness landscape, most of the sequence space can remain highly accessible owing to the indirect paths opened up by high dimensionality.
source: Our work demonstrates that even in the most rugged regions of a protein fitness landscape, most of the sequence space can remain highly accessible owing to the indirect paths opened up by high dimensionality.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a demonstration from the work.

claim: Throughout the course of infection, HIV always seems to find a way to revert to the global consensus sequence after immune invasion.
source: For example, throughout the course of infection HIV always seems to find a way to revert to the global consensus sequence, a putatively "optimal" HIV-1 sequence after immune invasion (Zanini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as an example and supported by a citation (Zanini et al., 2015).

claim: The sequence of a large protein may never be trapped in adaptation.
source: For example, it is plausible that the sequence of a large protein may never be trapped in adaptation (Gavrilets, 1997), so that adaptive accessibility becomes a quantitative rather than qualitative problem.
evidence: This is stated as a plausible scenario and supported by a citation (Gavrilets, 1997).

claim: The detection limit of fitness (w) in this system is ~0.01.
source: We previously determined that the detection limit of fitness (w) in this system is ~0.01 (Olson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by a citation (Olson et al., 2014).

claim: The fitness landscape was completed by imputing fitness values of the 10,639 missing variants using a model that incorporated main effects of single mutations, pairwise interactions, and three-way interactions among sites 39, 41 and 54.
source: The fitness landscape was completed by imputing fitness values of the 10,639 missing variants (i.e. 6.6% of the sequence space) that had fewer than 10 sequencing read counts in the input library. Our model of protein fitness incorporated main effects of single mutations, pairwise interactions, and three-way interactions among site 39, 41 and 54 (see Materials and methods, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Regularized regression with predictor selection based on biological knowledge was used to ameliorate possible bias in the inferred fitness landscape.
source: We used predictor selection based on biological knowledge, followed by regularized regression, which has been demonstrated to ameliorate possible bias in the inferred fitness landscape (Otwinowski and Plotkin, 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by a citation (Otwinowski and Plotkin, 2014).

claim: When mutations conferring larger fitness gains were more likely to fix, adaptation favored direct moves toward the destination, leading to shorter adaptive paths.
source: Consistent with previous studies (Orr, 2002, 2003), when mutations conferring larger fitness gains were more likely to fix (e.g. Greedy Model and Correlated Fixation Model), adaptation favored direct moves toward the destination, thus leading to a shorter adaptive paths (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Orr, 2002, 2003) and Figure 4C-D.

claim: The strength of selection interacts with the topological structure of fitness landscapes to determine the length and directness of evolutionary trajectories.
source: This suggests that the strength of selection interacts with the topological structure of fitness landscapes to determine the length and directness of evolutionary trajectories.
evidence: This is stated as a suggestion based on the findings.

claim: Many mutational trajectories involving extra-dimensional bypass did not fully commit to a fitness peak until the last two steps.
source: Consistent with this expectation, our simulations showed that many mutational trajectories involving extra-dimensional bypass did not fully commit to a fitness peak until the last two steps (Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 4.

claim: The constraints from the genetic code decreased the number of accessible variants due to the reduction in connectivity.
source: The constraints from the genetic code decreased the number of accessible variants due to the reduction in connectivity.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The reduction in connectivity from genetic code constraints did not alter the core finding that indirect paths substantially increase evolutionary accessibility.
source: However, this reduction in connectivity did not alter our core finding that indirect paths substantially increase evolutionary accessibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The observed higher-order epistasis was, at least partially, due to the steric effect among sites 39, 41, and 54.
source: We postulated that the observed higher-order epistasis was, at least partially, due to the steric effect among site 39, 41, and 54. This was evidenced by the enrichment of beneficial variants when the total volume of these three interacting residues was between ~200 Å3 and ~300 Å3.
evidence: This is stated as a postulation and supported by evidence from Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Entropic effect and conformational effect in IgG-FC binding may also contribute to higher-order epistasis.
source: Nonetheless, we acknowledged that entropic effect and conformational effect in IgG-FC binding may also contribute to higher-order epistasis.
evidence: This is explicitly acknowledged as a possibility.

claim: The global structure of the fitness landscape is influenced by the imputed fitness values of missing variants, which can vary when different fitness models or fitting methods are used.
source: Even in our system (with >93% coverage of the genotype space), the global structure of the fitness landscape is influenced by the imputed fitness values of missing variants, which can vary when different fitness models or fitting methods are used.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation.

claim: Measurement errors are expected to be very small due to the high reproducibility in the data.
source: Our analysis also ignored measurement errors, but the measurement errors are expected to be very small due to the high reproducibility in the data (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: The four amino acids chosen in the study are in physical proximity and have strong epistatic interactions.
source: Finally, we note that the four amino acids chosen in our study are in physical proximity and have strong epistatic interactions.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a note about the study design.

claim: The availability of conversion bypass only depends on the dimensionality at each site.
source: While the availability of conversion bypass only depends on the dimensionality at each site, the degree of higher-order epistasis and the availability of detour bypasses can be quite different in other fitness landscapes.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a general principle.

claim: The degree of higher-order epistasis and the availability of detour bypasses can be quite different in other fitness landscapes.
source: While the availability of conversion bypass only depends on the dimensionality at each site, the degree of higher-order epistasis and the availability of detour bypasses can be quite different in other fitness landscapes.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a caveat about generalizability.

claim: The details of a particular fitness landscape can influence the quantitative role of different bypass mechanisms, but this does not undermine the generality of the conceptual findings on extra-dimensional bypass, higher-order epistasis, and their roles in protein evolution.
source: Although the details of a particular fitness landscape can influence the quantitative role of different bypass mechanisms, this does not undermine the generality of our conceptual findings on extra-dimensional bypass, higher-order epistasis, and their roles in protein evolution.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a conclusion about the generalizability of the findings.

claim: Pairwise epistasis is prevalent in fitness landscapes.
source: Empirical evidence suggests that pairwise epistasis is prevalent in fitness landscapes (Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011; Kouyos et al., 2012; O'Maille et al., 2008; Lozovsky et al., 2009).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations (Kvitek and Sherlock, 2011; Kouyos et al., 2012; O'Maille et al., 2008; Lozovsky et al., 2009).

claim: Sign epistasis between two loci is known to constrain adaptation by limiting the number of selectively accessible paths.
source: Specifically, sign epistasis between two loci is known to constrain adaptation by limiting the number of selectively accessible paths (Weinreich et al., 2006).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by a citation (Weinreich et al., 2006).

claim: Previous empirical studies on combinatorially complete fitness landscapes have been limited to subgraphs of the sequence space consisting of only two amino acids at each site (2L genotypes).
source: Previous empirical studies on combinatorially complete fitness landscapes have been limited to subgraphs of the sequence space consisting of only two amino acids at each site (2L genotypes) (Weinreich et al., 2006; Lunzer et al., 2005; O'Maille et al., 2008; Lozovsky et al., 2009; Franke et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations (Weinreich et al., 2006; Lunzer et al., 2005; O'Maille et al., 2008; Lozovsky et al., 2009; Franke et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2011).

claim: Mutational reversions can occur during adaptive walks in diallelic sequence spaces such that adaptation proceeds via indirect paths.
source: However, it has also been shown that mutational reversions can occur during adaptive walks in diallelic sequence spaces such that adaptation proceeds via "indirect paths" (DePristo et al., 2007; Berestycki et al., 2014; Martinsson, 2015; Li, 2015; Palmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations (DePristo et al., 2007; Berestycki et al., 2014; Martinsson, 2015; Li, 2015; Palmer et al., 2015).

claim: In sequence space with higher dimensionality (20L), the extra dimensions may further provide additional routes for adaptation.
source: In sequence space with higher dimensionality (20L, for a protein sequence with L amino acid residues), the extra dimensions may further provide additional routes for adaptation (Gavrilets, 1997; Cariani, 2002).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Gavrilets, 1997; Cariani, 2002).

claim: The existence of indirect paths has been implied in different contexts, but it has not been studied systematically and its influence on protein adaptation remains unclear.
source: Although the existence of indirect paths has been implied in different contexts, it has not been studied systematically and its influence on protein adaptation remains unclear.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: Higher-order epistasis (interactions among more than two loci) has received much less attention and its role in adaptation is yet to be elucidated.
source: Higher-order epistasis (i.e. interactions among more than two loci) has received much less attention and its role in adaptation is yet to be elucidated (Weinreich et al., 2013; Palmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Weinreich et al., 2013; Palmer et al., 2015).

claim: When an extra dimension is introduced, a local maximum may become a saddle point and allow for further adaptation – a phenomenon known as extra-dimensional bypass.
source: Intuitively, when an extra dimension is introduced, a local maximum may become a saddle point and allow for further adaptation – a phenomenon that is also known as "extra-dimensional bypass" (Gavrilets, 1997; Cariani, 2002; Gutiérrez and Maere, 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Gavrilets, 1997; Cariani, 2002; Gutiérrez and Maere, 2014).

claim: Two distinct mechanisms of bypass were observed: conversion bypass (using an extra amino acid at the same site) and detour bypass (using an additional site).
source: With our experimental data, we observed two distinct mechanisms of bypass, either using an extra amino acid at the same site or using an additional site, that allow proteins to continue adaptation when no direct paths were accessible due to reciprocal sign epistasis (Figure 2).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by Figure 2.

claim: If the sequence space is limited to 2 amino acids at each site, the number of neighbors is 2; however, if all 20 possible amino acids were considered, the total number of neighbors would be 38.
source: If the sequence space is limited to 2 amino acids at each site, as in past analyses of adaptive trajectories, the number of neighbors is 2; however, if all 20 possible amino acids were considered, the total number of neighbors would be 38.
evidence: This is explicitly stated with the calculation provided.

claim: A successful conversion bypass requires that the original reciprocal sign epistasis is changed to sign epistasis after the conversion.
source: This bypass is feasible only if the original reciprocal sign epistasis is changed to sign epistasis after the conversion.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a requirement for conversion bypass.

claim: The enhanced accessibility mediated by indirect paths may provide a partial explanation for some observations in viral evolution.
source: The enhanced accessibility mediated by indirect paths may provide a partial explanation for some observations in viral evolution.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a potential implication of the findings.

claim: Adaptive accessibility becomes a quantitative rather than qualitative problem when the sequence of a large protein may never be trapped in adaptation.
source: For example, it is plausible that the sequence of a large protein may never be trapped in adaptation (Gavrilets, 1997), so that adaptive accessibility becomes a quantitative rather than qualitative problem.
evidence: This is stated as a plausible scenario and supported by a citation (Gavrilets, 1997).

claim: The bottleneck in experimental throughput has been improved substantially by coupling saturation mutagenesis with deep sequencing.
source: Recently, the bottleneck in experimental throughput has been improved substantially by coupling saturation mutagenesis with deep sequencing (Fowler et al., 2010; Hietpas et al., 2011; Jacquier et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2014; Thyagarajan and Bloom, 2014; Qi et al., 2014; Stiffler et al., 2015), which opens up unprecedented opportunities to understand the structure of high-dimensional fitness landscapes (Jiménez et al., 2013; Pitt and Ferré-D'Amaré, 2010; Payne and Wagner, 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is a huge gap between the limited throughput of fitness measurements (usually on the order of 102 variants) and the vast size of sequence space.
source: Nevertheless, there is a huge gap between the limited throughput of fitness measurements (usually on the order of 102 variants) and the vast size of sequence space.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a challenge in the field.

claim: The study does not aim to extrapolate protein fitness to organismal fitness.
source: We note that this study does not aim to extrapolate protein fitness to organismal fitness.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: There are examples showing that protein fitness in vitro correlates with organismal fitness in vivo.
source: Although there are examples showing that protein fitness in vitro correlates with organismal fitness in vivo (Natarajan et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2012), this relation may not be linear and is likely to be system-specific due to the difference in selection pressures in vitro and in vivo (Pál et al., 2006; Hingorani and Gierasch, 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Natarajan et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2012; Pál et al., 2006; Hingorani and Gierasch, 2014).

claim: The relation between protein fitness in vitro and organismal fitness in vivo may not be linear and is likely to be system-specific.
source: Although there are examples showing that protein fitness in vitro correlates with organismal fitness in vivo (Natarajan et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2012), this relation may not be linear and is likely to be system-specific due to the difference in selection pressures in vitro and in vivo (Pál et al., 2006; Hingorani and Gierasch, 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by citations (Pál et al., 2006; Hingorani and Gierasch, 2014).

claim: A total of 29 subgraphs were identified in which the quadruple mutant was the only fitness peak.
source: We identified a total of 29 subgraphs in which the quadruple mutant was the only fitness peak.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: Each subgraph is combinatorially complete with 24 = 16 variants, including WT, the quadruple mutant, and all intermediate variants.
source: Each subgraph is combinatorially complete with 24 = 16 variants, including WT, the quadruple mutant, and all intermediate variants.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the text.

claim: The analysis was limited to direct paths of adaptation, where each step would reduce the Hamming distance from the starting point (WT) to the destination (quadruple mutant).
source: By focusing on these subgraphs, we essentially limited the analysis to direct paths of adaptation, where each step would reduce the Hamming distance from the starting point (WT) to the destination (quadruple mutant).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a methodological choice.

claim: 19.7% of the measured genotypes are lethal (fitness=0).
source: 19.7% of the measured genotypes are lethal (fitness=0).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The fitness rank of the wild type genotype is 2.4% in the distribution of all fitness measurements.
source: The fitness rank of the wild type genotype is 2.4% in the distribution of all fitness measurements.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: There were 89,075,246 paired-end reads obtained for the input library and 45,587,128 paired-end reads obtained for the post-selection library.
source: There were 89,075,246 paired-end reads obtained for the input library and 45,587,128 paired-end reads obtained for the post-selection library.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Raw sequencing data have been submitted to the NIH Short Read Archive under accession number: BioProject PRJNA278685.
source: Raw sequencing data have been submitted to the NIH Short Read Archive under accession number: BioProject PRJNA278685.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The fitness of each variant is computed relative to WT (VDGV), such that the fitness of WT equals 1.
source: Therefore, the fitness of each variant, wi, could be viewed as the fitness relative to WT (VDGV), such that = 1.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The fraction of all possible variants that passed the filter was 93.4% (149,361 out of 160,000 all possible variants).
source: The fraction of all possible variants that passed this filter was 93.4% (149,361 out of 160,000 all possible variants).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The fitness of each single substitution variant was referenced to a previous study because the sequencing coverage was much higher in that study.
source: The fitness of each single substitution variant was referenced to our previous study (Olson et al., 2014), because the sequencing coverage of single substitution variants in our previous study was much higher than in this study (~100 fold higher).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation (Olson et al., 2014).

claim: The fitness of each single substitution in this study was calculated by multiplying a factor of 1.159 by the fitness of that single substitution computed from the previous study.
source: Subsequently, the fitness of each single substitution in this study was calculated by multiplying a factor of 1.159 by the fitness of that single substitution computed from our previous study (Olson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section and supported by a citation (Olson et al., 2014).
